query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a high-entropy alloy designed with titanium and nickel as the major constituents, a minor aluminum addition followed by an appropriate aging heat treatment will induce the in situ formation of a fine, coherent ordered γ′ precipitate phase within the FCC matrix, thereby improving the alloy’s yield strength and high‐temperature specific strength compared to the alloy without the aluminum addition by promoting effective precipitation hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy composed of at least five elements (each within 5–35 at%) with a predominantly single-phase FCC structure and without dedicated precipitation-hardeners.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of aluminum into the baseline Ti-Ni primary HEA and apply an optimized post-deposition aging heat treatment to promote a controlled precipitation of the γ′ phase.
generation.conditions: Alloy compositions must satisfy the high-entropy criteria; processing should be via methods such as direct energy deposition with subsequent aging at elevated temperatures to enable controlled precipitate formation without promoting excessive grain growth.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, uniformly distributed, and coherent ordered γ′ precipitate phase (for example, a nickel-titanium intermetallic or a related intermetallic) within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The fine γ′ precipitates act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion via precipitation hardening, thereby enhancing yield strength and strength retention at elevated temperatures while maintaining acceptable ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified Ti-Ni primary HEA, the aluminum-modified and aged alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in yield strength (e.g., an estimated improvement on the order of 20–30%) at elevated temperatures, leading to higher specific strength retention.
generation.baseline: The original Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy produced under identical processing conditions without the aluminum addition and subsequent aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The intervention is only applicable within the compositional boundaries of high-entropy alloys (each element 5–35 at%) and when processed by techniques (e.g., DED) that permit controlled thermal treatments; the added aluminum must not exceed levels that would form excessive intermetallics or deleteriously affect ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of yield strength improvement and the optimal Al content depend on processing details, precipitate size/distribution, and aging parameters; these factors introduce uncertainty in the precise quantification of property gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti-Ni primary HEA samples: one set as the control (without aluminum) and another set with a 5 at% aluminum addition. Process all samples under identical conditions using direct energy deposition (or a comparable method). Apply the same optimized aging heat treatment designed to promote γ′ precipitate formation in the aluminum-containing samples. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM and XRD to verify the presence, size, and distribution of the γ′ precipitates. Then, perform elevated-temperature tensile tests (e.g., at temperatures between 800 °C and 1123 °C) to measure yield strength and ductility.
measurements: SEM/TEM imaging and XRD phase analysis to assess precipitate formation and microstructure
Elevated-temperature tensile tests to determine yield strength, specific strength, and ductility
Statistical comparison of mechanical properties between the control and Al-added samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-added, aged alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 15% increase) in yield strength at elevated temperatures relative to the control and/or if the microstructural analysis fails to detect a notable, uniformly distributed γ′ phase, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of elements with similar metallic atomic radii but different crystallographic structures (Al and Ti) to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy caused higher solution strengthening by the element with a different crystallographic structure than the solvent. The solid solution strengthening coming from addition of 5 at. pct Al to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy is negligible, while the addition of 5 at. pct of Ti significantly increases the solid solution strengthening. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the addition of 5 at. pct Ti is comparable with the total effect of the 5 at. pct Al and 5 at. pct Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi). Precipitation hardening is much greater in the investigated alloys than the solid solution hardening. We showed a successful way for effectively strengthening the FCC-HEA system (NiCoFe) using a small Ti addition. The microstructure obtained in the M3 alloy consists of precipitates with an L12 structure and structurally coherent with FCC matrix. We showed one of the ways of searching for new high-entropy alloys.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was deposited using DED. The phase diagram of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was analyzed in terms of the deposition of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti. For the DED of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, powders of each element were mixed to prepare a mixed Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti powder, and this was deposited on SUS 304 substrates. The powders of each element of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA were mixed and deposited on substrates. The microstructure, tensile strength, and hardness of the deposited Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti alloy were measured. The primary findings of this study are as follows: As a result of the phase analysis of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, the γ phase of the FCC structure appeared as a matrix phase in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, and the γ′ phase of the ordered FCC structure additionally appeared. In addition, the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, designed with optimal values, was found to not appear in the precipitated phases other than the γ + γ′ phase. The matrix phase of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA appeared as the γ phase of the FCC structure, and the γ′ phase of the aligned FCC structure was confirmed to be widely dispersed in the form of dots similar to pores.
